The night sky has always held an irresistible pull. On clear evenings, away from city lights, the Milky Way spills across the darkness like spilled milk, each star a distant sun possibly nurturing worlds of its own. I find myself wondering about the light that left those points of brilliance millions of years ago, traveling through emptiness only to strike my eyes in this precise moment. Time collapses; the past becomes present.

Ancient navigators read those same patterns to cross oceans. Myths grew around the constellations—hunters, queens, dragons—because humans need stories to make sense of the infinite. Today our tools are sharper: radio telescopes listen for whispers from the early universe, space probes photograph the rings of Saturn in exquisite detail, and algorithms sift through petabytes of data for Earth-like exoplanets. Yet the fundamental emotion remains unchanged. Awe is not diminished by knowledge; it deepens.

Curiosity is the engine. Without it we would never have left the savanna, never built ships or rockets. It is also the quiet force behind every poem, painting, and late-night conversation. Standing under the stars, I feel both insignificant and essential—a temporary arrangement of atoms that can contemplate the whole.

There is practical value too. Understanding cosmic rays, solar weather, and orbital mechanics protects satellites and astronauts. More importantly, the habit of looking upward trains the mind to question, to connect distant dots, to stay humble. In an age of screens and schedules, that upward glance remains free, available to anyone who steps outside and simply looks. The universe does not demand credentials; it only asks for attention.
